newsitem.title: USA: Democrats try to diffuse controversy over funds.
newsitem.headline: Democrats try to diffuse controversy over funds.

text.p: Democrats, seeking to diffuse a crisis over alleged campaign financing violations, released data on Tuesday on donations that they initially planned to file only after the U.S. election on November 5.

But the move failed to placate Republicans, who threatened legal action to get Democrats to release a final report and urged Attorney General Janet Reno to appoint an independent counsel to investigate allegations the Democrats accepted improper foreign donations.

The Democratic National Committee late on Tuesday sent the Federal Election Commission (FEC) "an informational filing" of some 500-odd pages detailing its October contributors, reversing its earlier decision that it would not release the data until after the presidential election.
"Nobody is trying to hide anything," Representative Bill Richardson, a Democrat from New Mexico, told CNN's "Crossfire" programme.

The DNC's decision to release the "raw data" came shortly after Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour National called a news conference to say his party would ask a federal court for an injunction to freeze Democratic spending until they file an overdue report on donations and spending.

Democratic Party Chairman Christopher Dodd, a senator from Connecticut, responded by saying the party was not legally required to file a financial report before the election, but would file the preliminary report with the FEC, followed by an official final report "as soon as possible."

A sceptical Barbour, Dodd's Republican counterpart, said on CNN he did not expect to see the final report until after the election. There was no indication the Democratic gesture would lead Republicans to withdraw their legal challenge.
Earlier, Dodd said the decision not to file the report on the party's contributions and outlays by last Thursday's deadline had been made by staff members.

"If you don't make contributions then you don't legally have to file a report and so some staff made that decision. In my view they were wrong, you should file it even if you don't have expenditures because we're in that kind of environment," he told CNN.

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, on the campaign trail in Denver, said the flip-flop was typical for the Clinton administration. "You never get it all in this administration the first time," he said.
Barbour has suggested the failure to disclose the finances suggested the Democrats were hiding something.
The dispute follows news reports that Clinton's campaign was taking questionable contributions from people linked to financial interests in Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan.

The Justice Department is looking into reports that the chairman of the American Institute in Taiwan -- the U.S. diplomatic link with Taiwan -- urged Taiwanese businessmen to contribute to Clinton's re-election campaign.

Meanwhile John Huang, a key figure in allegations of improper Democratic Party fund-raising from Indonesian interests, was questioned in a civil suit by a conservative group seeking information about Huang's activities while he was a U.S. Commerce Department official.
